steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The lighthouse on Blackthorn Point had no neighbors, only the sea and the wind and the thin white beam that swept the dark like a watchful eye. Eamon, its keeper, lived alone in the stone tower, moving by habit through its narrow stairways and echoing rooms.

Every evening, just before dusk, he wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, checked the oil, and listened for the familiar sigh as the light flared to life. To anyone watching from afar, it was a simple routine. To Eamon, it was a conversation.

“Steady now,” he would murmur, running a hand along the cool metal rail. “Storm’s coming in from the south.”

The sea answered by flinging spray against the base of the cliffs. The glass panes rattled. Far out, the clouds piled into a gray wall, their undersides lit faintly by the dying sun. Eamon could smell the storm: salt, rain, and the sharp metal scent of lightning waiting to fall.

He had once been a sailor. His right leg still ached when the weather turned, a souvenir from the night a wave had torn him from the deck of the Halcyon and dashed him against a half-seen rock. The lighthouse’s beam that night had been a thin needle of hope in a world of black water and roaring wind. He had crawled to its base at dawn, half-conscious, and woken in a cot with bandages wrapping his ribs like another man’s arms.

The old keeper, a quiet woman named Marta, had poured him broth, shook her head at his gratitude, and said only, “The light did the work. I just keep it burning.”

He had stayed. At first to heal, then to help, then because he could not think of anywhere else he wanted to be.

Years later, after Marta’s hands began to tremble and her eyes clouded, she left in a small mailboat and did not return. The tower felt too large that winter, every empty room an echo of her slow, careful footsteps. Eamon signed his name in the ledger as the new keeper and tried to ignore how his hand shook.

The townspeople on the mainland thought him strange. They called him “the ghost of Blackthorn” and crossed themselves when the lighthouse appeared as a pale tooth between waves. To them, the lamp was an old machine in an age of modern ships and electric charts. Necessary, perhaps, but fading.

To Eamon, it was neither old nor new. It simply was. A promise of return, cast into the dark.

On the night the storm truly came, the wind did not howl so much as roar, a continuous low thunder that shook every stone. Rain sheeted sideways, becoming one with the spray. The beam of the lighthouse stabbed outward and immediately dissolved into a gray blur.

The radio on Eamon’s desk crackled with fragments of voices.

“…dead in the water…”

“…engine failure… visibility zero…”

“…need bearings… any light… any—”

He adjusted the frequency with careful fingers. “…Vessel, this is Blackthorn Point Light. Say your name.”

After a moment, the reply came, broken but clear enough. “Fishing trawler Marigold. Lost bearing. We can’t see the headland. We… we don’t know which way is safe.”

Eamon closed his eyes, letting his mind see the charts he’d stared at for years. The layout of shoals and hidden teeth of rock. The pattern of the currents, the way the sea clawed at ships driven too far east.

“You’re four miles off my beam,” he said. “When you see the light, keep it to your port side, not dead ahead. That’ll put you in clear water. Speed slow. Acknowledge.”

Static hissed, then: “Acknowledge. We’ll look for you, Blackthorn.”

The phrase lodged in his chest unexpectedly. We’ll look for you. As if he were not a man alone in a tower, but a star in the sky.

Minutes crawled. The storm worsened. Twice, the lamp’s flame trembled, almost went out. Eamon tightened the vents, shielded it with his body. The tower shuddered as a wave hurled itself up the cliff and against the stones.

His right leg burned as though the sea were inside it again. He gritted his teeth and climbed each step anyway, up and down, checking the lens, the fuel, the rotation. The storm tried to smear the light away; he answered by making it brighter.

Finally, far below, through the broken curtain of rain, he saw it: the faint yellow suggestion of a cabin light, then the ghostly shape of a hull rising and falling. For a heartbeat, the Marigold seemed aimed straight at the cliffs.

“Port, you fools,” he whispered, even though they could not hear. “Port.”

On the water, the little light shifted, veering. The trawler angled away, scraping past the hidden teeth of rock that had taken so many hulls and so many men. Eamon watched until the pinprick of light crawled out into wider, safer water, where the sea still heaved but did not claw.

The radio crackled again, weaker now, but jubilant. “Blackthorn, this is Marigold. We’ve cleared the shoals. Would’ve been kindling on those rocks without you. Can’t see you, but… thank you.”

Eamon looked at the great lens rotating around him, its glass facets catching the flame and throwing it outward. He thought of Marta, and the night the lighthouse had found him in the water. He thought of the town, and the way people pretended not to look at the beam when it swept by.

“You saw me well enough,” he said into the microphone. “Safe travels home.”

When the storm finally spent itself, dawn came dressed in bruised colors: deep purples fading to yellow along the horizon. The sea was littered with foam and broken branches, but the cliffs still stood, and the lighthouse with them.

Eamon made his morning round. He checked the glass for cracks, wiped away salt, noted a loosened bolt in the log. Habits, all of them, but they held the day together. As he finished, he paused at the window facing the town.

Far away, across the water, he could just make out the harbor. Tiny masts. The faint shape of buildings. A thread of smoke.

Something else moved there—small glints of light, one after another, as if someone on shore were holding up mirrors to the rising sun. It took him a moment to understand.

They were signaling.

Not in code, not in patterns, not in any language he knew. Just brief, irregular flashes, like hands waving from far, far away. Like people saying, We know you’re there. We see you.

Eamon watched for a long time. Then he smiled, light and tentative, and rested his forehead against the cool glass.

“Steady now,” he told the tower, and perhaps himself. “They’re looking back.”

That evening, as the sun slid down and the sea turned to ink, the lamp at Blackthorn Point ignited. The beam swept out across the dark water, over shoals and hidden rocks and the safe channel home, turning in its slow, patient circle.

On the logbook’s new page, under the date, Eamon wrote in neat letters: Light exhibited at dusk. Visibility good. One vessel guided through storm. Keepers present: 1.

He hesitated, then added a single word.

Witnesses: many.
